questions.question: What happens to your endpoints when you add spring-boot-starter-security and write no configuration?
questions.explanation: Spring Boot secures every URL by default and prepares a user with a generated password.

questions.question: Which bean describes which URLs are open and which need a login?
questions.explanation: A SecurityFilterChain bean holds the request rules and the login method.

questions.question: The rules are: requestMatchers("/public/**").permitAll() then anyRequest().authenticated(). A caller with no login requests /public/hours and then /appointments. Which status codes come back?
questions.explanation: The public URL matches the first rule and is allowed, while /appointments needs a login and returns 401.

questions.question: A developer writes anyRequest().authenticated() first and requestMatchers("/public/**").permitAll() after it. The public pages still ask for a login. Why?
options: Rules are matched from top to bottom and the first match wins
Public pages need a second filter chain
questions.explanation: The catch-all rule at the top matches every request first, so the later permitAll rule is never reached.

questions.question: A tutorial tells you to extend WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter, but the class cannot be found in your Spring Boot 4 project. What is the current approach?
options: Add an older Spring Security jar
Write a servlet filter by hand for every URL
questions.explanation: The adapter class was removed, and modern Spring Security uses SecurityFilterChain beans.
